title: Two segregated locals with different scales; the Josephine Baker bind
summary: Black Local 208 and white Local 10 had different scales; hiring Local 10 accordion and violin players for Josephine Baker at the Regal brought Saunders trouble.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, you were involved in union affairs through the years, Local 208.
Yeah.
Was the black local, had two locals here in Chicago.
Right, right.
And Local 10, the one local, and Local 208, the black. The union -- the black union has always been very strong in the music business of the black musicians, hasn't it?
Well, it was, yeah.
It was a gathering point.

Well, it was a -- I think we spoke a little bit before, you said social -- there was an amount of sociability within the union beside the business aspects of the union. They were very sociable. Musicians were pretty close together, everybody knew practically everybody. And so
it made it a pretty nice thing. But the only thing about the two unions in the same jurisdiction, they just did not have the same rules and regulations.
Different scales or --

Right, this is what I'm saying. The scales were different, and I got caught, boy, in a real bind with -- we played Josephine Baker, and her instrumentation required accordians. She was from Europe. And it required accordians and maybe some terrific fiddle players that came through.
And so, I had to go and hire some of the musicians from Local 10. And the two scales was entirely different. And I run into a real donnybrook about that thing. I got my head bashed in for it.
When was this?
This was in 1960, I think. Yeah.
Well, your band at the Delisa was -- had some white musicians in it occasionally.
Oh, yeah, but that was fine. But, see, the only thing about this is Petrello and Gray were holding hands.
Well, that was always the story, that they had an agreement.
They had an agreement, definitely so. They had this agreement, and then when I come up and hired
these musicians in the Regal and then the musicians went to their union to find out what the scale was, and they gave them one thing and then out here it was something else.
What was the outcome of it? You had to pay the higher scale?

Well, I paid -- the guys were very, very nice. They were very nice, and they said, well, Red, whatever you do is all right. So I think it was a thing -- in between I paid them, and they took it very, very -- Local 208 took it very -- a very bad attitude toward me. They didn't like this. They didn't like -- but it wasn't the integrating of the bands so much as it was for me pulling the cover off of Local 208 as to what they were doing.
Well, what do you mean, what were they doing?
Well, I mean, their scales were lower than 10's, and they were supposed to be having the same scales.
